25.1 i ntroduction
In the previous chapter, we developed a measure for the degree of correspondence or
relationship between two variables. These types of statistics provide information about the
degree and, sometimes, the direction of the relationship. However, we can go beyond cor-
relation analysis to predict, with known accuracy, the value of one of the variables when the
value of the other is known. This prediction process is called regression.
The word “regression” comes from the first study that used the concept, which was published
by Sir Francis Galton in 1885.
1
In the study, Galton examined the relationship between
heights of parents and their children and found that the heights of children of unusually tall
or short parents tended toward the average height of the population; that is, their heights
regressed toward the average height. Regression has come to mean the prediction of the
value of a variable from the values of one or more other variables.
Consider the simplest case, in which we have collected value pairs for two variables, X and Y,
and we wish to predict the value of Y that might correspond to a given value of X.
We have seen that a scatter diagram graphically illustrates the relationship between two vari-
ables, and a linear relationship exists if the data points of the scatter diagram appear to clus-
ter around a straight line. We know how to develop methods to identify the line that comes
closest to all the data points, that best summarizes the apparent relationship between X and
Y. This line is called the regression line, and we can predict the value of Y

Regression analyses serve three purposes in statistical research: description, statistical con-
trol, and prediction. In some situations, previously collected data is examined to discover the
relationship between some dependent quantity and one or more independent variables. In
these cases, description is the goal.
In a study of the relationship between two variables, the researcher can use regression analy-
sis to statistically control the influence of some other quantity. For example, in a study of two
marketing strategies, surveys might be administered after each quarter. Regression equa-
tions can be found to relate the marketing strategy performance ratings to sales personnel,
and these equations can be used to adjust the ratings, inflating those sales personnel with
limited field experience and deflating those sales personnel with years of field experience.
Remaining differences in performance ratings are then due to differences in the two market-
ing strategies.
Finally, a regression equation can be used to predict the value of a variable from the value of
some other quantity, as in predicting sales averages from amount of advertisement funding.

Companies whose products are based upon software development are concerned with the
amount of code developed in a project as well as the development time needed. Clearly, the
relationship between lines of code and function points, or a weighted average of the soft-
ware’s information domain and assessments of the software complexity, depends upon the
programming language utilized and the quality of the software design.
An excellent article, complete with an associated data file, for developing a linear regres-
sion model that uses function points to predict development time is by Jack E. Manson
and Brian R. Haggard in the Journal of Statistics Education, Vol. 15, Nov. 2 (2007) found
at http:/www.amstat.org/publications/jse/v15n2/datasets.matson.html. This text can be freely
shared among individuals.

using historical function point data. In developing a useful regression model, a number of

function points.

A company is one of the largest volume specialty retailers of consumer electronics, personal
computers, entertainment software, and appliances. In August of each year, the company
purchases mainframe MIPS (Millions of Instructions Per Second, a measure of computing
resources) in anticipation of the coming holiday season. Computing resources are needed
to track and analyze retail information needed for billing, inventory, and sales. For planning
and budgeting purposes, they also wish to forecast the number of MIPS needed the follow-
ing year.
You are asked to forecast the MIPS needed for December 2000 and December 2001 using
the company dataset. This dataset contains monthly data on computer usage (MIPS) and
total number of stores from August 1996 to July 2000. Additionally, information on the
planned number of stores through December 2001 is available.
After carefully studying the article:
a. Plot the computer usage versus time using SPSS and interpret the results.
b. Study the following concepts for forecasting models using MAD and CFE:
The evaluation of forecasting models is based on the desire to produce forecasts that are
unbiased and accurate. The Mean Absolute Deviation (MAD) is one common measure of
forecast accuracy.

a. Calculate forecasts using a three-period moving average and exponential
smoothing with a smoothing constant of 0.2.
b. Calculate the MAD and CFE for both models. Determine the “best model.”
